Watch this rock. It's an octopus.
It can change its colors in as little as a fifth of a second. That's about as fast as a blink.
How? Its skin is full of millions of tiny bags of color.
Each bag holds a single color, like yellow, red or brown.
Tiny muscles pull a bag wide open, like stretching a balloon. When they let go, it shrinks back to a dot.
Nerves from the brain tell the muscles when to pull. That's why it's so fast.
But the bags can't make blue or green. So under them are shiny cells that bounce those colors back.
And under those are white cells. They take on the color of the light around them.
Color is not enough. Rocks are bumpy. So the octopus pushes up little bumps to make its skin rough.
Here's the strange part. Most scientists think octopuses are color-blind.
So how does it match? Nobody knows for sure.
Here's a clue: in a test, a bit of octopus skin in a dish reacted to light, with no eyes or brain. But it was slow, and nobody knows if it helps.
So that's color bags, shiny cells, white cells and bumps.
Next time you see a rock, look twice.
